item.text: {"text":"Closest recent match: [2Gated-TimeGRU, HICSS 2024](https://aisel.aisnet.org/hicss-57/da/data_science/10/), which incorporates consecutive interaction intervals into GRU updates to model short-term preferences and temporal dynamics. Earlier [T-GRU recommendation work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598) similarly introduces temporal gates into recurrent state transitions. A lightweight decay mechanism comes from [GRU-D](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-24271-9): jointly learn γ = exp(−ReLU(WΔt+b)), then multiply the previous hidden state by γ before the GRU update. Its evidence concerns clinical time series, not purchases; missingness assumptions should not transfer automatically. [GRUwE, TMLR 2026](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=YLoZA77QzR), provides newer evidence that relatively simple recurrent architectures remain competitive for irregular next-observation/event prediction, without establishing gains on this Amazon benchmark.\n\nSuggested experiment, inferred from these mechanisms: retain one jointly trained GRU4Rec per category; compare ordinary GRU, log1p-gap input conditioning, and a small learned per-dimension state-decay gate. Initialize retention near one and constrain decay slopes nonnegative if monotonic forgetting is intended. Use only observed history timestamps; never require the unknown next-purchase time. Proposed controls: constant gaps, shuffled gaps with item order preserved, and removal of older history prefixes. These distinguish useful temporal alignment from extra parameters or generic recency effects; they do not establish that gaps reveal intent. Preserve padding masks, final-nonpadding readout, and identical timestamp processing in training and prediction. Select by the fixed four-category macro validation HR@10; no cited result establishes improvement under that evaluator."}
